narrative:
The prediction that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt was central to the denial. The model estimated a 59% probability of failure, meaning that, based on the information considered, you were seen as more likely to fail than to pass. This does not mean failure is certain, but it placed you in a high-risk category for the law school’s admission standards. The decision was not based on your gender, race, or family income.

The strongest signal was your class standing in the third year. Being in the lowest decile indicates a downward academic trajectory relative to accepted applicants, whose average third-year decile was close to the middle. This weighed heavily toward the failure prediction. The second most influential factor was your undergraduate GPA, and here the news was positive: at 3.60, it is above the average of 3.23 among accepted students, so it pushed the prediction toward passing. However, this positive influence was not enough to overcome the other risks. The third major factor was your LSAT score. At 26, it is well below the average of 37.18, and this strongly pushed the prediction toward bar exam failure, since lower LSAT scores are associated with lower first-time bar passage rates.

To improve your chances, focus on retaking the LSAT to raise your score substantially, and consider applying to programs with academic support or bar-exam preparation resources. A stronger LSAT score and evidence of improved academic performance could change a future outcome.
